title_en: Fragments on the Letter to the Philippians
author: Oecumenius
occasion: Fragmentary comments on Philippians, preserved in catenae, explaining difficult phrases and the letter's purpose.
argument: Paul writes to clergy to cultivate humility, since pride especially afflicts those who live well. Paul's sufferings and defenses are shown to be fruitful through the Philippians' faith and steadfastness. The phrase 'as a man' expresses intensity, not mere likeness. Paul counts his former gains as loss only by comparison with the superiority of better things. The law is like a stalk whose refuse was once necessary for the seed to grow, but now circumcision, Sabbath-keeping, and similar things are separated as refuse, while the pure wheat of faith is stored in the master's barns.

outline.move: The letter is addressed to clergy, and its main aim is to instill humility, since pride especially attacks those who live well.

Paul's sufferings and defenses are shown to be fruitful through the Philippians' faith, and several phrases are explained: 'as a man' means intensity, 'holding fast' means paying attention, and former gains are counted as loss only by comparison with what is better.

The image of refuse as part of the stalk is developed: just as refuse once helped the seed grow, so the law, prophets, and hidden proclamation of Christ grew from the seed of Abraham's faith, with the harvest at Christ's first coming.

The law's stalk has not ceased, but circumcision, Sabbath-keeping, and the rest are separated like refuse, while the pure wheat of faith is stored away; Paul's forgetting what lies behind means not dwelling on past struggles but focusing on what lies ahead.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle and author of the letter to the Philippians.

cast.name: Timothy
cast.who: Paul's co-worker, mentioned as receiving similar advice about paying attention to oneself.

cast.name: Euodia
cast.who: A woman in Philippi; some say she is the wife of the jailer, though this is a reported opinion, not Oecumenius's own view.

cast.name: Syntyche
cast.who: A person in Philippi; some say Syntyche is 'the man' or husband, presented as a counterpart to Euodia, though this is a reported opinion.

cast.name: Abraham
cast.who: The patriarch whose faith is the seed from which the law, prophets, and Christ grew.

voices.speaker: Oecumenius speaking in Paul's voice
voices.how_marked: First-person paraphrase expanding Paul's thought, not direct quotation

key_terms.sense: Humility, the main virtue Paul seeks to cultivate in the Philippian clergy
Pride or self-inflation, the vice that especially attacks those who live well
The Philippians' steadfastness or firm stand in faith, used as proof of Paul's fruitful suffering
Refuse or dung, part of the stalk, once useful for the seed to grow but now separated and set aside
Stalk or straw, representing the law and prophets that grew from the seed of Abraham's faith
Ear of grain, representing Christ hidden and proclaimed in advance
Seed, representing Abraham's faith from which the law, prophets, and Christ grew
Harvest, representing the first coming of the Savior when the threshing floor is cleansed
Threshing, the separation of grain from refuse at Christ's first coming
Wheat, the pure grain of faith hidden in the prophetic stalk and stored in the master's barns
Barn or storehouse, where the pure wheat of faith is gathered by the common master
Clergy, the specific audience of the letter as opposed to laity
Laity, the non-clerical members of the church, contrasted with the letter's actual audience

scripture: The author cites Philippians by standard book name and chapter/verse. Old Testament references use LXX forms: Psalm 72:1 (LXX) corresponds to Psalm 73:1 in modern numbering; Psalm 118:97 (LXX) corresponds to Psalm 119:97. Cite as 'Ps 73:1 (LXX 72:1)' and 'Ps 119:97 (LXX 118:97)'.
uncertain: The exact date of Oecumenius's work
Whether the identification of Euodia as the jailer's wife and Syntyche as 'the man' reflects Oecumenius's own view or only a reported opinion
The precise extent of the original commentary from which these fragments derive
Whether Syntyche is identified as the husband of Euodia or simply as a male figure

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul counts his former gains as loss only by comparison with the superiority of better things
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἦν ζημία, ἀλλὰ κατὰ παράθεσιν τῆς ὑπερβολῆς τῶν κρειττόνων ἡγεῖται ζημίαν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paul counts his former gains as loss only by comparison with the excess/superiority of better things; the source emphasizes that they were not actually bad things (κέρδη, gains) but are reckoned as loss by way of comparison (κατὰ παράθεσιν)

_unresolved_facts.claim: The law is like a stalk whose refuse was once necessary for the seed to grow
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τοῦτο οὖν τὰ σκύβαλον ποτὲ χρησιμώτατον εἰς τὸ τεχθῆναι τὸν σπόρον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The refuse (σκύβαλον) was once most useful for the seed to be born/grow; but the analogy is more complex: from Abraham's faith as seed came the root/law, the stalk/prophets, and the ear of grain/Christ secretly proclaimed, with harvest at Christ's first coming

_unresolved_facts.claim: The image of refuse as part of the stalk is developed: just as refuse once helped the seed grow, so the law, prophets, and hidden proclamation of Christ grew from the seed of Abraham's faith, with the harvest at Christ's first coming
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὡσπερεὶ ἀπὸ σπόρου ἡ ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν νόμῳ, καὶ ἡ καλάμη τῶν προφητῶν καὶ ὁ στάχυς ἤδη τὸν Χριστὸν ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ προκαταγγέλλων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The image is: from Abraham's faith as seed came the root (those in the law), the stalk (prophets), and the ear of grain (Christ already secretly proclaimed); the refuse is not the stalk itself but a part of the stalk, and the harvest separates wheat from refuse

_unresolved_facts.claim: The law's stalk has not ceased, but circumcision, Sabbath-keeping, and the rest are separated like refuse
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὔτε λοιπὸν ἐπαύσατο μὲν ἡ καλάμη τοῦ νόμου, ὡσπερ δὲ σκύβαλον ἐχωρίσθη περιτομή, σαββάτων τήρησις καὶ τῶν ἄλλων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The stalk of the law has NOT ceased (οὔτε...ἐπαύσατο), but circumcision, Sabbath-keeping, and the rest are separated like refuse; the brief's 'has not ceased' is correct but the phrasing 'The law's stalk has not ceased' could be clearer that this is the source's point

_unresolved_facts.claim: Syntyche is 'the man' or husband, presented as a counterpart to Euodia, though this is a reported opinion
_unresolved_facts.fix: Syntyche is identified as 'the man' (τὸν ἄνδρα), not 'the husband' specifically; the Greek ἄνδρα means 'man' (male person), and the brief's 'husband' is an interpretive leap not in the source

_unresolved_facts.claim: Oecumenius speaking in Paul's voice, how_marked: First-person paraphrase expanding Paul's thought, not direct quotation, sections: u01-rem-early
_unresolved_facts.fix: The first-person voice in u01-rem-early is Paul's own words from Philippians 1:7 (ἀπὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας πίστεως ἀπόδειξιν ποιοῦμαι τὴν ὑμετέραν ἔνστασιν) — this is direct quotation of Paul, not Oecumenius speaking in Paul's voice; the second part is third-person commentary about Paul

_unresolved_facts.claim: Psalm 72:1 (LXX) corresponds to Psalm 73:1 in modern numbering; Psalm 118:97 (LXX) corresponds to Psalm 119:97
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὡς ἀγαθὸς ὁ θεὸς τῷ Ἰσραήλ, καὶ ὡς ἠγάπησα τὸν νόμον σου, κύριε
_unresolved_facts.fix: The citations are: Psalm 72:1 (LXX) = Psalm 73:1 MT ('ὡς ἀγαθὸς ὁ θεὸς τῷ Ἰσραήλ'); Psalm 118:97 (LXX) = Psalm 119:97 MT ('ὡς ἠγάπησα τὸν νόμον σου, κύριε'). However, the brief's 'Ps 73:1 (LXX 72:1)' format is reversed — it should be 'LXX 72:1 = MT 73:1' or 'Ps 72:1 LXX'
